result: The authors demonstrate that LytM and lysostaphin (LSS) have similar substrate specificities and both prefer the D-Ala-Gly cross-linked part of mature peptidoglycan. However, while LSS is genuinely a glycyl-glycine hydrolase, LytM can also act as a D-alanyl-glycine endopeptidase.
evaluation: All reviewers affirm this as a major finding. The editor states 'The authors show that LytM has a novel function of cleaving D-Ala-Gly instead of only Gly-Gly' and one reviewer notes 'The major finding is that LytM is not only a Gly-Gly endopeptidase, but also cleaves D-Ala-Gly.' Another reviewer describes the results as 'very convincing and demonstrate that the enzymatic properties of the model enzymes studied need to be revisited.'

result: The authors show that LSS hydrolyzes pentaglycine 15-fold faster than LytM in vitro, and both enzymes are highly specific for the bond between Gly2 and Gly3 (>85-94%) when cleaving pentaglycine, with residual cleavage activity towards the bond between Gly3 and Gly4 (<15%).
evaluation: Reviewers describe the experimental approach as 'robust' and providing 'a thorough analysis of LSS and LytM enzymatic activities.' The editor notes the use of 'compelling NMR-based real-time kinetics measurements.' No concerns are raised about these kinetic findings.

result: The authors demonstrate through NMR kinetics that both LytM and LSS prefer mature PG fragments containing a D-Ala-Gly cross-link between two stem peptides. Cross-linking L-Lys-D-Ala dipeptide N-terminally to pGly increased the rate of hydrolysis by factors of 12 and 8 for LSS and LytM, respectively. The enzymes show different responses to N-terminal and C-terminal modifications of the substrate.
evaluation: One reviewer states 'The experimental strategy and its implementation are robust and provide a thorough analysis of LSS and LytM enzymatic activities. The results are very convincing.' Another reviewer notes 'the experimental work is extremely well designed and way beyond what people usually do in the field.' No concerns are raised about these kinetic measurements.

result: The authors show that in cross-linked substrates, LSS hydrolyzes amide bonds between Gly1-Gly2 and Gly2-Gly3 with preference for the first one, while LytM can cleave both the D-Ala-Gly1 amide bond and the Gly1-Gly2 bond. This dual activity of LytM was confirmed with both synthetic substrates and muropeptides extracted from S. aureus sacculus.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the findings as 'very convincing' and note that 'the enzymatic properties of the model enzymes studied need to be revisited.' The editor highlights this as a 'novel function' of LytM. One reviewer acknowledges that 'the authors have addressed most of my concerns' regarding the biological significance.

result: The authors demonstrate that both enzymes can hydrolyze substrates with reduced numbers of glycines in the cross-bridge (femB and femAB mutant mimics). LSS can hydrolyze substrate 9 (with only a single glycine) by cleaving the Lys Nζ-monoGly CO isopeptide bond, though at drastically lower rates. LytM maintains activity with serine substitutions at different positions, showing greater flexibility than LSS.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the experimental work as 'extremely well designed' and the results as 'very convincing.' One reviewer notes 'This work is addressing a real gap in our knowledge since very little information is available about the substrate specificity of peptidoglycan hydrolases.' No concerns are raised about these findings.

result: The authors provide a comprehensive substrate specificity model showing that LSS is a strict glycyl-glycine endopeptidase with P1 and P1' positions invariably occupied by Gly residues, while LytM is flexible at the P1 site (accommodating either D-Ala or Gly). The structural basis for these differences is explained by loop 1 length differences between the enzymes, with molecular modeling supporting the mechanistic interpretations.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the quality of the work, with one stating 'I think the experimental work is extremely well designed and way beyond what people usually do in the field. I believe that this sets a precedent that is worth acknowledging.' The integration of kinetic data with structural modeling is implicitly accepted without criticism.

result: The authors show that LytM is a S. aureus PG hydrolase with a catalytic M23 domain structurally very similar to that of LSS, as demonstrated by structural comparison.
evaluation: This structural similarity is accepted by reviewers as background context for the study. One reviewer notes the enzymes are 'structurally highly homologous' and no concerns are raised about this characterization.
